# The Problem

When working in R, it's already common to have standard conventions for code style: packages like [lintr](https://lintr.r-lib.org/) [@hester2025] and tools like [air](https://posit-dev.github.io/air/) and [jarl](https://jarl.etiennebacher.com/) are widely used to ensure that code conforms to agreed standards.
Documentation doesn't receive the same attention.
While `R CMD check` verifies that documentation exists and matches usage, there is no common tooling for ensuring that docs are readable by a human, whether that is the help pages, vignettes and READMEs read by users or the code comments read by contributors, and this responsibility falls to authors and reviewers.

Documentation that is hard to read, whether because of dense sentences or a tone that assumes things are obvious, increases cognitive load [@sweller1988], frustrates users, and can be a real barrier to adoption.

Organisations like rOpenSci recognise this, and their [software review process](https://devguide.ropensci.org/) asks reviewers to judge whether documentation is clear and sufficient.
The problem is also growing: R packages are increasingly written with the help of, or exclusively by, AI tools, and without oversight it's easy to end up with verbose documentation.

Some prior work exists. The [docreview](https://github.com/thisisnic/docreview) package, on CRAN between 2021 and 2024, contained 5 checks including readability scores, but stalled due to the complexity of its architecture. The [spelling](https://docs.ropensci.org/spelling/) package checks words but not prose.
Outside of R, [Vale](https://vale.sh) is a mature documentation linter with prose rules and packaged style guides, which runs in editors and on CI. It handles Markdown and can extract the text of comments from R source files, but it has no knowledge of R package structure or R vocabulary, its built-in styles flag function and argument names as spelling errors, and using it requires installing and configuring a separate binary outside of R.

The R ecosystem lacks an opinionated documentation linter, usable from R, that helps both humans and AI tools write better docs for R packages.
